Great Exchange
grayt eks-CHAYNJ
noun phrase (the doctrine of imputation in the cross)
A Reformation phrase (Luther's admirabile commercium, “wonderful exchange”) for the double imputation at the cross: our sin to Christ, His righteousness to us.

Biblical Definition

The great exchange is the Reformation name for the wonderful transaction at the cross in which our sin was reckoned to Christ and His righteousness reckoned to us. The apostle states it in a single verse of unfathomable depth: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” Here is a double imputation. Our sins were laid upon the sinless Christ—the LORD laid on Him the iniquity of us all—and He bore them as our substitute, the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God. And the perfect righteousness of Christ, His whole active and passive obedience, is credited to the believing sinner, so that by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. Nothing of our own merit enters the transaction; it is reckoning, not infusion—a change of standing before God, received by faith alone. Luther called it the admirabile commercium, the wonderful exchange: Christ takes what is ours (sin, guilt, condemnation, death) and gives us what is His (righteousness, sonship, acceptance, life). The dictionary holds the great exchange as the very marrow of justification: the sinner stands before God not in his own filthy rags but clothed in the righteousness of Another, accepted in the Beloved. To deny the imputation of Christ's righteousness, as Rome and some modern revisionists do, is to leave the sinner naked; to confess it is to glory in a salvation wholly of grace.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Reformation doctrine of the double imputation at the cross—our sin reckoned to the sinless Christ, His righteousness reckoned to us (2 Corinthians 5:21); the marrow of justification, received by faith alone.

expand to see more

GREAT EXCHANGE, noun phrase. [Luther's admirabile commercium, the wonderful exchange.] The double imputation at the cross.

Our sin was reckoned to Christ: He was made sin for us who knew no sin.

His righteousness is reckoned to us: that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him.

It is imputation, a change of standing, not infusion of an inherent quality.

Received by faith alone; the marrow of the doctrine of justification.

Key Scripture

2 Co 5:21 — "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him."

1 Pe 3:18 — "For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit:"

Isa 53:6 — "All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all."

Ro 5:19 — "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous."

Modern Corruption

Rome and the “new perspective” deny the imputation of Christ's righteousness, recasting justification as infused grace or covenant membership and leaving the sinner without the borrowed righteousness Scripture credits.

expand to see more

The Roman doctrine denies that the believer is justified by an imputed (reckoned) righteousness, teaching instead an infused righteousness that makes him inherently just by degrees, so that justification and sanctification are confused and assurance is lost. The dictionary rejects this on the plain word that we are made the righteousness of God in him—a righteousness that is His and credited to us, not ours by infusion. The great exchange is reckoning: Christ counted a sinner though He had no sin, we counted righteous though we have none of our own.

A subtler modern denial comes from the “new perspective” and allied revisionists, who recast justification as mere covenant membership or future vindication and deny that Christ's active obedience is imputed to the believer. This too the dictionary refuses. Romans 5:19 is explicit: by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. The whole obedience of Christ—His perfect keeping of the law and His penal death—is the righteousness reckoned to faith. Strip away the imputation and the sinner is left in his rags; confess it and he stands accepted in the Beloved, clothed in a righteousness not his own.

Hebrew Roots

From Luther's admirabile commercium (wonderful exchange); the doctrine rests on the Greek logizomai (to reckon, impute) and the “for us” (huper hemon) of substitution.

expand to see more

Admirabile commercium, Latin, “the wonderful exchange,” Luther's phrase for the cross.

Logizomai, Greek, to reckon, count, or impute, the verb of Romans 4 and 5.

Hamartian epoiesen, Greek, “he made him to be sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Dikaiosune Theou, “the righteousness of God,” the standing credited to the believer.

Huper, Greek, “on behalf of, in the place of,” carrying the substitution.

Usage

"The pastor preached the great exchange, that Christ took our sin and we receive His righteousness by faith alone."

"He answered Rome by showing that we are made the righteousness of God in Christ, a reckoned and not an infused righteousness."

"She rested her assurance not in her own rags but in the borrowed righteousness of the great exchange."
